title: Mourning Turned Into Celebration
overview: God promises the struggling people back from exile that Jerusalem will be peaceful, faithful and full of life again, that their days of mourning will become festivals, and that people from many nations will one day come to seek him there.

parts.label: God returns to Jerusalem (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: "Jealous" here means a fierce, protective love: the anger that once fell on the city now turns toward defending it. Jerusalem, once known for betraying God and its own people, will become known as a city of truth, faithful to God, and its temple hill will be called holy.

parts.label: Peaceful streets, scattered people home (vv. 4-8)
parts.note: Old people with canes and children playing outside picture a city where war and famine no longer cut lives short. The returned exiles saw mostly ruins and found this hard to believe, so God asks whether anything is too wonderful for him, and promises to gather his people from east and west, meaning from everywhere.

parts.label: Keep building (vv. 9-13)
parts.note: Around 520 BC the prophets Haggai and Zechariah urged the people to finish rebuilding the temple, after years of failed harvests, lost wages and danger on the roads. God promises good crops, and says Judah, whose name other nations had used as a curse, will become a name people use as a blessing.

parts.label: God's mind is made up (vv. 14-17)
parts.note: God says he is now as determined to do them good as he once was to punish their ancestors. In return he asks for honest speech, fair verdicts in the courts held at the city gates, no scheming against neighbors and no lying under oath.

parts.label: Fasts become feasts (vv. 18-19)
parts.note: This answers the question about fasting raised in chapter 7: these yearly fasts mourned the siege and fall of Jerusalem, the burning of the temple and, most likely, the murder of the governor Gedaliah afterward. God says these sad days will become joyful festivals, and asks the people to love truth and peace.

parts.label: The nations come seeking (vv. 20-23)
parts.note: People from many cities will urge each other to go to Jerusalem to seek God, and ten from every language will grab one Jewish person's robe, a gesture of eager pleading, because they have heard God is with them. Christians have often read this in light of the spread of faith in Jesus among non-Jewish peoples.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether these promises were fulfilled in the restored community and later in the worldwide church, or still await a future, literal fulfillment centered on Jerusalem and the Jewish people.
think: What would have to be true of a place for both the very old and the very young to feel safe in its streets?
